extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, history of science, and methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarises Francis Bacon's classes of 'instances' (instantiae) and methodological guidance for using them in natural inquiry — e.g., instances that aid memory, constitutive instances, conformable/analogical instances, monadic and deviant instances, and cautions about analogy. Useful for understanding methodological criteria for evidence and experiment in early-modern natural philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms that aid memory (sex Formae Minores)
rubrics_metrics.description: Six minor forms which assist memory (sex Formae Minores): abscissio infiniti; deductio intellectualis ad sensibile; impressio in affectu forti; impressio in mente pura; multitudo ansarum; praeexpectatio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each form is illustrated and explained: e.g., breaking the infinite into parts (abscissio infiniti); intellectual deduction to the sensible (deductio intellectualis ad sensibile, helpful in artificial memory); strong emotion producing impression (impressio in affectu forti); impressions laid on a pure, less-occupied mind such as childhood or before sleep (impressio in mente pura); multiplicity of circumstantial hooks such as writing in parts and loud recitation (multitudo ansarum); and expectation/attention improving retention (praeexpectatio). Example practice: reading a text many times and attempting recitation, consulting the book when memory fails. (Full list and examples given in text.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Constitutivae (Constitutive instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances which constitute or give a species/part — concrete observations that determine the nature or part-structure of a faculty or quality (e.g., examples showing that gustation is in part internal olfaction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to define species or parts and to indicate composite natures (for taste: cases of persons without olfaction, obstructed nares, or instantaneous perception on vigorous suction show taste involves internal olfaction and certain touch). These instances establish what the sense or quality essentially involves and are central to forming correct definitions and divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Conformes / Proportionates / Analogies
rubrics_metrics.description: Instances of conformity or proportion (analogies) are similarities and correspondences between objects or qualities that are dissimilar in many respects — 'Analogies' drawn from different domains that indicate likenesses in principle or structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies are highly fertile sources of suggestion for scientific and practical discovery (examples: telescope vs eye, basalt vs lava, comparative anatomy leading to the discovery of circulation). They help compare unknown formations to known ones to infer formation or principle. They are chiefly concerned with individual observations (not direct inductive generalisations) and often suggest axioms or direct inquiry. They can set the track for discovery but must be used in conjunction with rigorous logical method and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about analogies — accept only real/substantial similarities
rubrics_metrics.description: Only accept conformable instances/analogies that denote physical, real, substantial, and immersed similarities in nature — not fortuitous, superficial, superstitious, or merely curious correspondences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns against treating trivial or spurious resemblances (as in natural-magic writers) as scientific evidence. Conformable instances should indicate real natural likenesses that can guide to true axioms and laws; avoid accepting analogies that are accidental or merely speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority of collecting similarities and analogues over mere cataloguing of variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Scientific diligence should shift from merely noting the variety and minute differentiations of animals, plants, and fossils toward seeking and recording resemblances and analogues (integrals and parts) that unite nature and begin sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that cataloguing fine differences often yields curiosities rather than useful science; instead, workers should collect and investigate similarities and analogies (both in wholes and parts) because these reveal the unity and fabric of nature and are the basis of scientific knowledge. However, this practice must be accompanied by caution to avoid spurious analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Monodicae (Monadic / heteroclite instances)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monadic (monodicae, heteroclites) instances are concrete, extravagant, or apparently abrupt phenomena — singular or outlying cases within a genus (e.g., comets, double stars, peculiar metal behaviors) that seem not to fit ordinary kinds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their use is akin to clandestine instances: they raise and unite nature to find genera or common natures and prompt inquiry to discover the general form from which the singularity deviates. One should amass many such instances because they sharpen and vivify inquiry and remedy intellectual deformity caused by habitual observation. Investigate until the supposed miracle reduces to properties or relations of a common form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instantiae Deviantes (Deviating instances / errors of nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deviating instances are errors of nature, vagaries, or monsters where nature departs from ordinary course — 'miracles' of individuals rather than species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although similar in use to monadic instances, deviating instances correct the intellect against customary expectations and reveal hidden processes. The investigator should not cease inquiry until the cause of deviation is found; understanding the deviation often elucidates the ordinary processes and can lead to improved descriptions of natural ways (example: perturbations of Uranus leading to the discovery of Neptune).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule: investigate exceptions until they are explained by general law
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not accept exceptional or singular phenomena as inexplicable secrets; continue inquiry until irregularities are shown to depend on some common form or process (i.e., reduce exceptions to law where possible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly prescribes persistent investigation of anomalies (monodicae and deviant instances) with the expectation that many exceptions will ultimately be traceable to general laws or processes. Examples and historical notes (e.g., magnetism found in many metals, discoveries completing an apparent discontinuity) illustrate this rule.
